content: Loa loa is a species of filarial nematode, commonly referred to as the eye worm, that causes Loa loa filariasis in humans. Its geographic distribution primarily includes regions of Africa and India. This parasite is one of three filarial nematodes responsible for subcutaneous filariasis in humans, alongside Mansonella streptocerca and Onchocerca volvulus (the latter being the causative agent of river blindness). The maturing larvae and adult worms of Loa loa inhabit the subcutaneous fat layer of human skin, where they induce disease. The young larvae develop within horseflies of the genus Chrysops (commonly known as deer flies or yellow flies), including species such as C. dimidiata and C. silacea. These flies transmit the infection to humans through their bites. Morphology The body structure of Loa loa worms is relatively simple, consisting of a head, body, and tail. Female worms are larger, ranging from 20 mm to 70 mm in length and approximately 425 μm in width. Life Cycle The life cycle of Loa loa involves three key species: the parasite itself, the fly vector, and the human host. The process unfolds as follows: 1. A vector fly bites an infected human host, ingesting microfilariae (the early larval stage of the parasite). 2. The microfilariae migrate to the fat body of the insect host, where they develop sequentially into first-stage larvae, second-stage larvae, and finally third-stage larvae. 3. The infective third-stage larvae travel to the proboscis of the fly. 4. When the infected fly bites an uninfected human host, the third-stage larvae penetrate the skin and enter the subcutaneous tissue of the human. 5. Within the human host, the larvae mature into adult worms, which subsequently produce microfilariae. These microfilariae can be found in various bodily fluids and tissues, including peripheral blood, spinal fluid, urine, and the lungs. Pathogenesis Loa loa parasites infect humans by migrating through subcutaneous tissues, causing inflammation along their path. When a parasite temporarily halts its movement in a specific location, it triggers localized inflammation known as Calabar swellings. These swellings are characterized by tense, pruritic (itchy), inflammatory subcutaneous edema, often occurring near the joints of the extremities. They typically last for 1 to 3 days and represent areas of angioedema caused by the host's immune response to allergens released by the maturing worm and its metabolic byproducts. Calabar swellings are most commonly observed near the wrist and ankle joints and tend to resolve once the parasite resumes its movement. The parasites can also migrate to and infect the eye, leading to swelling and discomfort in the affected area. Common symptoms of Loa loa filariasis include itching, joint pain, fatigue, and, in severe cases, death. Diagnosis and Treatment The diagnosis of Loa loa filariasis is primarily based on the detection of microfilariae in the blood, the visual identification of a worm in the eye, or the observation of characteristic skin swellings. Surgical removal of the worm is a straightforward procedure when the parasite is visible and accessible. The most commonly used treatment for Loa loa filariasis is the antiparasitic drug ivermectin. While ivermectin is widely regarded as an effective treatment, it may leave behind a residual microfilarial load. In cases of high microfilarial loads, a course of ivermectin, prolonged administration of albendazole, or cytapheresis sessions may be employed to reduce the microfilarial burden and prevent severe adverse events. One such adverse event is fatal encephalopathy, which can occur due to the death of large numbers of microfilariae. Cytapheresis is a procedure that can reduce microfilarial loads by up to 75% and is particularly useful in cases of very high parasitic burden. Another treatment option, diethylcarbamazine, is effective against both microfilariae and adult worms. However, its use is associated with more severe side effects and carries a risk of fatal complications.
